questions.stem: In VCE Politics, a humanitarian crisis is best described as:
options: any dispute between two states over the terms of a trade agreement or the level of tariffs
a change of government that follows a free and fair national election in a large state
a natural event confined to a single small town that local emergency services are able to manage alone
an event or series of events that threatens the safety and wellbeing of large numbers of people
questions.explanation: The study design describes humanitarian crises as events that threaten the safety and wellbeing of communities or large numbers of people, from human rights abuses, armed conflict or mass movement. A trade dispute or a routine change of government does not meet that test.

questions.stem: A government strips citizenship from an ethnic minority, restricts its movement and allows attacks on its villages. Hundreds of thousands flee across the border. The main cause of this crisis is:
options: the collapse of the international financial system
ethnic discrimination and the denial of nationality
a conflict over trade between two neighbouring states
climate change driving the loss of rural livelihoods
questions.explanation: The scenario describes discriminatory state policies aimed at one group, which the study design names as a cause of human rights crises and mass movement. Nothing in it involves trade, climate or finance.

questions.stem: An armed group controls territory, collects taxes and attacks civilians across a border. In VCE Politics this group is classified as:
options: a regional grouping
an institution of global governance
a non-state actor
a state
questions.explanation: Even when an armed group controls territory, it lacks widely recognised sovereignty, so it is not a state. The study design lists terrorist groups and illegal groups among non-state actors.

questions.stem: Violence between a government's forces and an organised armed group within the same state is classed in international humanitarian law as:
options: an act of aggression between states
a dispute for the International Court of Justice
a non-international armed conflict
an international armed conflict
questions.explanation: International humanitarian law distinguishes international armed conflicts between states from non-international ones within a state. A crime of aggression involves one state's use of force against another.

questions.stem: Under current international human rights law, human rights are regarded as:
options: inherent, indivisible and universal
granted by states, divisible and conditional
inherent, divisible and limited to a state's citizens
universal but applicable only in times of peace
questions.explanation: The study design states that human rights are regarded as inherent, indivisible and universal, though not all states agree or meet their obligations. They belong to every person, not only citizens, and apply in war as well as peace.

questions.stem: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is best described as:
options: a General Assembly declaration that is not itself a binding treaty
a binding treaty that is enforced by the International Criminal Court
a Security Council resolution binding on every member of the United Nations
a regional charter of rights adopted by the states of the Council of Europe
questions.explanation: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly as a statement of common standards; its rights were later made binding in treaties such as the two 1966 covenants. The ICC tries individuals for atrocity crimes and does not enforce the UDHR.

questions.stem: Together with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which two 1966 treaties make up the International Bill of Human Rights?
options: the Rome Statute and the Geneva Conventions
the Genocide Convention and the UN Charter
the ICCPR and the ICESCR
the Refugee Convention and its Protocol
questions.explanation: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights were both adopted in 1966. The Refugee Convention dates from 1951 and its Protocol from 1967.

questions.stem: Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, what distinguishes genocide from other crimes against civilians?
options: intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group
the killing of more than a set number of civilians within a single armed conflict
attacks carried out by the armed forces of a state rather than by a rebel or militia group
acts committed during a war between two states rather than within one state
questions.explanation: Genocide is defined by the specific intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. There is no minimum number of deaths, and genocide can be committed by any actor in peace or war.

questions.stem: The rules of international humanitarian law, such as the Geneva Conventions, mainly aim to:
options: limit the effects of armed conflict by protecting civilians and those no longer fighting
decide which side in an armed conflict is legally in the right to use military force
ban states from using armed force against another state under any circumstances, even in self-defence
give refugees the right to resettle permanently in the state of their own choosing
questions.explanation: International humanitarian law regulates how wars are fought, protecting civilians, the wounded and prisoners whatever the cause of the war. Whether force may be used at all is governed separately by the UN Charter.

questions.stem: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a refugee is a person who:
options: has crossed a border mainly to find work with better wages and conditions
has fled armed conflict but has stayed inside the borders of their own state
has been granted citizenship and permanent residence by a second state
is outside their country owing to a well-founded fear of persecution
questions.explanation: The Convention defines a refugee as someone outside their country of nationality with a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. People displaced within their own state are internally displaced persons, not refugees.

questions.stem: People who flee armed conflict but remain inside their own state's borders are known as:
options: internally displaced persons
refugees under the 1951 Convention
stateless persons
asylum seekers
questions.explanation: Internally displaced persons have not crossed an international border, so they fall outside the Refugee Convention and remain under their own government's protection. A refugee by definition is outside their country.

questions.stem: A person who is not considered a national by any state under the operation of its law is:
options: stateless
an internally displaced person
an economic migrant
a resettled refugee
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a stateless person in the 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons. Statelessness often results from discriminatory nationality laws and leaves people without basic rights.

questions.stem: A state turns back a boat of asylum seekers to a country where they face a real risk of persecution. This would breach:
options: the principle of complementarity
the right of veto in the Security Council
the principle of non-interference
the principle of non-refoulement
questions.explanation: Non-refoulement, at the heart of refugee law, forbids returning people to a place where they face serious threats to their life or freedom. Complementarity is the principle governing when the ICC can act.

questions.stem: The main role of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is to:
options: prosecute individuals accused of crimes against humanity before its own tribunal
decide how many refugees each member state must accept under binding quotas
deploy armed peacekeepers to defend refugee camps from attack by militias
protect refugees and stateless people and help find durable solutions
questions.explanation: UNHCR works to protect displaced and stateless people, supports host states and helps find long-term solutions. It cannot force states to accept refugees, and it has no prosecutorial or military role.

questions.stem: UNHCR's three durable solutions for refugees are:
options: detention, deportation and resettlement in a third country
repatriation, offshore processing and temporary protection
integration, naturalisation and compulsory return home
voluntary repatriation, local integration and resettlement
questions.explanation: A durable solution ends a refugee's displacement: returning home voluntarily and safely, integrating into the host state, or resettling in a third state. Compulsory return would breach the principle of non-refoulement.

questions.stem: Herders in a drought-stricken region cross a border after losing their livestock and income. Why might they not qualify as refugees under the 1951 Convention?
options: Environmental hardship is not one of the Convention's grounds of persecution
The Convention protects only people who have travelled beyond a neighbouring state
The Convention covers only nationals of states that are parties to the Convention
Refugee status requires a separate Security Council resolution for each crisis
questions.explanation: The Convention's grounds are race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group and political opinion; drought and loss of livelihood are not among them. This gap is a challenge as climate change drives more movement of people.

questions.stem: Why is the cooperation of neighbouring states often critical to resolving a mass movement of people?
options: They usually host most of the people who flee
They alone have authority to grant refugee status under the Convention
They decide whether the ICC may open an investigation into the crisis
They hold a right of veto over the operations of UNHCR in the region
questions.explanation: Most people fleeing a crisis go first to neighbouring states, which then carry much of the cost of hosting them. Any state party can assess refugee claims, and the ICC's jurisdiction does not depend on neighbours' approval.

questions.stem: A neighbouring state hosting large numbers of refugees calls on wealthier, more distant states to resettle more of them and fund the response. Its argument appeals mainly to the principle of:
options: burden- and responsibility-sharing
the principle of non-refoulement
the principle of complementarity
the principle of non-interference
questions.explanation: Burden- and responsibility-sharing, the central idea of the 2018 Global Compact on Refugees, holds that hosting refugees is a shared international responsibility. Non-refoulement is tempting, but it concerns not returning refugees to danger rather than who carries the cost.

questions.stem: The Responsibility to Protect (R2P), endorsed at the 2005 World Summit, applies to which four crimes?
options: war crimes, aggression, torture and slavery in all their forms
crimes against humanity, corruption, terrorism and genocide
genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity
genocide, terrorism, piracy and international drug trafficking
questions.explanation: R2P covers only these four mass atrocity crimes. It is not a general licence to intervene over other problems such as terrorism or corruption.

questions.stem: Under the third pillar of R2P, if a state manifestly fails to protect its population, the international community should be prepared to take collective action:
options: through any coalition of willing states, without UN authorisation
through armed forces under the command of the International Criminal Court
only after the state concerned has formally consented to the action
through the Security Council, in line with the UN Charter
questions.explanation: The 2005 World Summit agreed that collective action would be taken through the Security Council in accordance with the Charter, including Chapter VII. Action under Chapter VII does not require the consent of the state concerned.

questions.stem: After Security Council Resolution 1973 (2011) authorised measures to protect civilians in Libya, Russia, China and others argued that the intervention became a campaign for regime change. This perspective mainly reflects concern about:
options: the erosion of state sovereignty and non-interference
the cost to donor states of funding UNHCR refugee camps
the narrow jurisdiction of the ICJ over individual leaders
the absence of any human rights provisions in the UN Charter
questions.explanation: Critics feared that R2P could be used as a pretext to overthrow governments, undermining sovereignty and the norm of non-interference. This experience has since made some permanent members more reluctant to authorise action in other crises.

questions.stem: Only five states can block a Security Council resolution with a single negative vote. They are:
options: China, Germany, India, Japan and the United States
France, Japan, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States
China, India, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States
China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States
questions.explanation: The Security Council has 15 members, but only the five permanent members hold a veto. The ten elected members serve two-year terms and have no veto.

questions.stem: A draft resolution imposing sanctions on a state committing atrocities receives 13 votes in favour, one against and one abstention. The vote against is cast by a permanent member. The resolution:
options: passes, but takes effect only as a recommendation to UN members
is sent on to the General Assembly to be decided by a binding vote
fails, because a negative vote by a permanent member is a veto
passes, because it has more than the nine affirmative votes required
questions.explanation: A substantive resolution needs nine affirmative votes and no negative vote from any permanent member. However many members support it, a single permanent member voting against defeats it.

questions.stem: A permanent member abstains on a draft resolution that receives 11 votes in favour and none against. The resolution:
options: fails, because twelve affirmative votes are needed for any resolution
passes only once the General Assembly has also approved it by majority
passes, because by long practice an abstention is not treated as a veto
fails, because every permanent member must vote in favour for it to pass
questions.explanation: Although the Charter speaks of the concurring votes of the permanent members, long-standing Council practice treats an abstention as not blocking a resolution. With 11 votes in favour, more than the nine required, it passes.

questions.stem: A permanent member vetoes action against a state that buys its weapons and hosts one of its naval bases. This best illustrates:
options: an R2P response carried out under the third pillar
national interests blocking a collective response to a crisis
the principle of complementarity limiting the ICC's role
the success of preventive diplomacy in avoiding conflict
questions.explanation: The study design notes that attempts to resolve conflicts are often blocked by perceptions of the national interest. The veto lets one permanent member protect an ally and its own strategic interests.

questions.stem: The International Criminal Court differs from the International Court of Justice in that the ICC:
options: can try only the nationals of the permanent Security Council members
tries individuals, whereas the ICJ hears disputes between states
hears disputes between states, whereas the ICJ tries individuals
is a principal organ of the UN, whereas the ICJ is independent of it
questions.explanation: The ICC, set up under the Rome Statute, prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. The ICJ is the UN's principal judicial organ and settles legal disputes between states.

questions.stem: The ICC acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute. This is the principle of:
options: complementarity
universality
non-refoulement
collective security
questions.explanation: Under complementarity, national courts have the first responsibility to prosecute atrocity crimes and the ICC is a court of last resort. Non-refoulement belongs to refugee law.

questions.stem: Atrocities are committed by a state's own forces entirely within its territory, and that state is not a party to the Rome Statute. The ICC can generally act only if:
options: the state accepts its jurisdiction or the Security Council refers the situation
the ICJ first rules that the state has breached the Genocide Convention
a majority of the General Assembly votes to authorise an investigation
a neighbouring state that hosts refugees from the crisis requests it
questions.explanation: The ICC's jurisdiction rests on crimes occurring on a party's territory or by a party's nationals, a state's acceptance, or a Security Council referral. A referral can be vetoed, which is a major challenge to accountability.

questions.stem: ASEAN's response to a humanitarian crisis inside one of its member states has often been limited by:
options: its standing army, which only the Security Council is able to deploy
its rule that all members must accept every refugee from the crisis
its long-standing principle of non-interference in members' internal affairs
its requirement that every member state be a multi-party democracy
questions.explanation: Non-interference is a founding principle of ASEAN and is written into its Charter, which makes it reluctant to pressure a member over internal matters. ASEAN has no standing army and no democracy requirement.

questions.stem: Unlike ASEAN, the African Union's founding Constitutive Act gives it the right to intervene in a member state in respect of:
options: any change of government brought about by election
disputes over tariffs and trade between members
a member's refusal to adopt a common currency
war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity
questions.explanation: The Constitutive Act gives the AU a right to intervene in grave circumstances, namely war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. This contrasts with ASEAN's stronger emphasis on non-interference.

questions.stem: Which non-state actor is known for its neutrality, its role as guardian of international humanitarian law and its visits to detainees in armed conflicts?
options: the World Food Programme
the International Committee of the Red Cross
Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders)
Human Rights Watch
questions.explanation: The ICRC is a neutral, impartial and independent humanitarian organisation with a special role under the Geneva Conventions. Médecins Sans Frontières is also a neutral humanitarian NGO, but it delivers medical care rather than acting as guardian of the Geneva Conventions, and the World Food Programme is a UN agency rather than a non-state actor.

questions.stem: Non-government organisations such as Human Rights Watch mainly respond to crises by:
options: voting on Security Council resolutions as an official observer
documenting and publicising abuses to pressure governments to act
deploying armed personnel to protect civilians in conflict zones
prosecuting offenders in a tribunal that the NGO itself runs
questions.explanation: Human rights NGOs gather evidence, publish reports and lobby states and institutions, using information and public pressure rather than force. They have no vote in the Security Council.

questions.stem: Which is an example of diplomacy being used to address a crisis?
options: a peacekeeping force patrolling a buffer zone between armed groups
an NGO airlifting medical supplies into a besieged town
a regional envoy negotiating a ceasefire between warring parties
an international court convicting a militia leader of war crimes
questions.explanation: Diplomacy is negotiation between actors to manage or resolve a dispute, as an envoy brokering a ceasefire does. A court conviction is a legal process, and peacekeeping is a military response.

questions.stem: A neutral third party helps warring sides reach their own agreement but cannot impose a decision on them. This process is:
options: intervention
mediation
arbitration
adjudication
questions.explanation: A mediator facilitates negotiation but has no power to decide the outcome. In arbitration and adjudication, a third party makes a decision that the parties have agreed to accept or that is legally binding.

questions.stem: Traditional UN peacekeeping rests on three principles:
options: neutrality, secrecy and an unlimited right to use armed force
Security Council consent alone, partiality and deterrence
consent of the parties, impartiality and limited use of force
regime change, disarmament and military occupation of territory
questions.explanation: UN peacekeeping relies on the consent of the main parties, impartiality, and no use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Peacekeepers do not aim to change regimes.

questions.stem: In humanitarian action, the principle of impartiality means that aid is given:
options: on the basis of need alone, without discrimination
only to civilians on the side of the recognised government
in equal amounts to every party involved in the conflict
only once a ceasefire agreement has formally been signed
questions.explanation: Impartiality requires aid to go to those in greatest need, regardless of nationality, ethnicity, religion or politics. Equal shares for each side would ignore differences in need.

questions.stem: Targeted sanctions freeze the assets of a regime's leaders, but the regime continues its abuses, sustained by trade with a large neighbouring state. This best shows that sanctions:
options: are unlawful under international law unless the ICJ has approved them first
always harm ordinary civilians far more than they harm the regime's leaders
work only when they are combined with the resettlement of refugees abroad
depend on wide participation, because other actors can offset their effects
questions.explanation: Sanctions lose force when other states keep trading with the target, so their effectiveness depends on broad cooperation. Targeted sanctions are designed to limit harm to civilians, so it is not true that they always hurt civilians most.

questions.stem: The government of a state accused of abuses calls the matter an internal security operation and rejects outside criticism, while UN investigators call for accountability. These positions reflect a tension between:
options: sovereignty and the universality of human rights
non-refoulement and burden-sharing among hosts
complementarity and the veto of permanent members
deterrence and the principle of collective security
questions.explanation: The accused government appeals to sovereignty and non-interference, while investigators appeal to universal human rights that do not stop at borders. This tension is one of the main challenges to resolving human rights crises.

questions.stem: A peace agreement ends the fighting but leaves armed group leaders in power and does not return displaced people. An analyst would most likely say the agreement has produced:
options: change, because displaced people have been returned safely to their homes
short-term stability without addressing the underlying causes of the crisis
lasting change, because the root causes of the conflict have been resolved
renewed instability, because the fighting resumed on a larger scale
questions.explanation: The end of fighting brings a measure of stability, but unresolved grievances and continuing displacement mean the causes remain. Stability and change must be judged against the causes of the crisis, not just whether fighting has paused.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that a global response to an armed conflict was effective?
options: A large number of Security Council meetings held to discuss the conflict
A General Assembly resolution passed to condemn the violence on both sides
Generous pledges of aid announced at an international donor conference
A sustained fall in civilian deaths and the safe return of displaced people
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is measured by outcomes for the people affected, such as fewer deaths and safe returns. Meetings, resolutions and pledges show activity and concern, but not that the crisis has actually eased.

questions.stem: In a mass movement crisis, a receiving state stresses border security while a refugee NGO stresses the rights of asylum seekers. These differences arise mainly because:
options: only NGOs are permitted to assess claims for refugee protection
the actors bring different interests and values to the same crisis
the NGO is bound by the Refugee Convention but the state is not
border security is prohibited under international refugee law
questions.explanation: Perspectives are shaped by each actor's interests and values: a state weighs security and domestic politics, while an NGO focuses on human rights. Only states can be parties to the Refugee Convention, and states may control their borders consistently with non-refoulement.
